title: Launch a Student Hackathon Demo in 48 Hours
steps: Hour 0–1: Define scope and success metrics — decide event type (virtual, in-person, hybrid), target audience size, demo length per team, judging criteria, prize structure, and minimum viable deliverables.
Hour 1–2: Assemble core team and assign roles — event lead, logistics, tech lead, communications, volunteer coordinator, judge coordinator, safety/legal point of contact.

Hour 2–4: Lock logistics and tools — reserve venue or streaming platform, pick primary video conferencing + backup, set up registration form, and create a single upload location for demos (Google Drive, Dropbox, or submission portal).

Hour 4–6: Publish a concise announcement — include date/time, who can participate, registration link, demo requirements, judging rubric, code of conduct, and contact info. Use email lists, social media, campus groups, and partner orgs.

Hour 6–10: Open rapid registration and triage teams — collect team names, contact person, project short descriptions, tech needs, and demo preference (live vs pre-record). Cap or waitlist if needed and confirm final number by T-24h.

Hour 10–14: Recruit judges and mentors — invite faculty, local engineers, alumni; share judging rubric, time per demo, scoring form (Google Form or Sheet), and compensation or recognition. Confirm availability windows.

Hour 14–18: Set up communication channels — create Slack/Discord/WhatsApp channels for announcements, a help desk channel for tech support, and a volunteer/organizer channel. Share links with participants and volunteers.

Hour 18–24: Technical rehearsals and templates — provide participants with demo template (2–5 slide/1-minute intro + 5–7 minute demo), submission naming convention, and how-to for screen share or pre-record upload. Run a volunteer tech test of all platforms.
T-24h: Final confirmation sweep — email all teams, judges, volunteers with schedule, login links, timelines, and contact phone numbers. Gather any final tech requirements or accessibility needs.

T-18–12h: Create minute-by-minute runbook — include check-in times, demo order, buffer slots, intro/welcome script, transitions, judge scoring deadlines, tie-break policy, and award announcement timing.

T-12–6h: Prepare backups and contingency plans — for each demo slot allow a pre-recorded video; have spare laptops and dongles; set up a moderator to start/stop timers; prepare backup judges or remote judging form.
T-6–3h: Run full dress rehearsal with volunteers and one or two volunteer teams — test screen sharing, audio, video recording, live streaming, judging form flow, and projected scoreboard updates.

T-3–1h: Final participant check-in and support — confirm each team can access required platforms, collect final submission links, remind of code of conduct and demo etiquette, and distribute final schedule.
Event start and execution: Follow the runbook strictly, keep timeboxes, monitor tech channels, have a live tech support person, collect scores immediately after each demo, and record sessions.

Post-event (immediately after): Tally scores, announce winners, share recordings and feedback forms, send thank-you notes to judges/volunteers, and publish a short wrap-up with next steps and ways to stay involved.
Post-event (24–72h): Collect and publish results, distribute prizes, archive submissions, summarize lessons learned with organizers, and update a short postmortem for future events.
risks: Low registration or no-shows — mitigated by targeted outreach, waitlist, and confirming attendees at T-24h.
Platform or internet failure during demos — mitigate with backups: pre-recorded demos, alternate video links, and spare hardware/internet tethering.
Judge no-shows or inconsistent scoring — mitigate by over-recruiting judges, sharing a clear rubric, and using a standardized scoring form.
Schedule slippage — mitigate with strict timekeeping, a stage manager to enforce times, and buffer slots between demos.
Insufficient technical support — ensure dedicated tech volunteers, test runs, and clear escalation paths.
Copyright/privacy issues with demo content — require participants to confirm rights or anonymize sensitive data and provide guidance on permissible content.
Plagiarism or non-original work — require brief provenance statements, use honor code, and include a vetting step for top finalists.
Venue or in-person safety issues (if physical) — have emergency contacts, basic first aid plan, venue access checks, and COVID/health policy reminders.
Data loss or missing submissions — enforce submission deadlines, make redundant backups, and confirm receipt when possible.
Poor demo quality or unfair advantage (pre-built products) — clarify what qualifies as a hackathon demo in rules, and reserve the right to disqualify entries that violate rules.
